objectives.text: Understand the origin of elements and the chemical evolution of living systems.
Appreciate the various atomic models and the periodic properties of elements.
Explain the types and importance of chemical bonds in biomolecule formation.
Explain enzyme function, classification, and factors affecting enzyme function.
Understand the biological role of carbohydrates, proteins, nucleic acids, and lipids.

concepts.title: Elements, atoms and biological organisation
concepts.learningGoals: Distinguish an element from an atom, ion and isotope. Use proton number to identify an element, and explain why knowing the elements in a cell does not yet explain how that cell works.

concepts.title: Where biological elements came from
concepts.learningGoals: Compare early-universe nucleosynthesis, stellar processes and laboratory synthesis. Separate the origin of nuclei from the later origin of chemical compounds and living cells.

concepts.title: Major elements, trace elements and essentiality
concepts.learningGoals: Recognise CHONPS as a useful biological grouping. Distinguish abundance, essentiality and chemical form, and interpret composition comparisons without turning them into dietary advice.

concepts.title: Why carbon supports diverse biological structures
concepts.learningGoals: Explain tetravalency and catenation. Compare carbon with silicon and boron without assuming that belonging to the same periodic-table region makes elements biologically interchangeable.

concepts.title: Biological selection from the periodic table
concepts.learningGoals: Explain why environmental abundance is insufficient to predict cellular composition. Evaluate “chemical democracy” as a descriptive phrase and distinguish explanatory evidence from resemblance.

concepts.title: Mineral roles, exposure and toxic interference
concepts.learningGoals: Connect selected elements with specific biological roles. Distinguish normal function from toxic interference and recognise when a source statement needs qualification rather than a confident clinical answer.

concepts.title: Living systems as organised open systems
concepts.learningGoals: Explain why energy flow, organisation and inherited information must be considered together when describing life. Distinguish a useful characteristic from a complete definition.

concepts.title: Habitability and evidence for origin models
concepts.learningGoals: Separate conditions that permit chemistry from evidence that life exists. Distinguish modern atmospheric conditions from uncertain early-Earth models.

concepts.title: Origin hypotheses and controlled experiments
concepts.learningGoals: Distinguish historical spontaneous generation, panspermia and chemical-origin hypotheses. Explain what a contamination-control experiment can establish.

concepts.title: From simple reactants to organic precursors
concepts.learningGoals: Interpret the Miller experiment without claiming it created life. Distinguish synthesis of a base or amino acid from synthesis of a complete nucleotide, protein or cell.

concepts.title: Polymer formation, hydrolysis and activation
concepts.learningGoals: Explain why assembling useful polymers requires more than a supply of monomers. Distinguish a simplified condensation representation from actual energy-coupled biosynthesis.

sections.title: Connecting monomers is a chemical problem

concepts.title: Templates, RNA and the information problem
concepts.learningGoals: Distinguish information storage from catalysis. Explain the importance and limits of catalytic RNA in origin-of-life models.

concepts.title: Compartments and protocell models
concepts.learningGoals: Compare micelles, vesicles and coacervate droplets. Explain how compartmentalisation can help and constrain a developing chemical system.

concepts.title: Early metabolism and evolutionary pathways
concepts.learningGoals: Explain how connected reactions and environmental resources can support persistence. Distinguish plausible metabolic-development models from established historical sequences.

concepts.title: Atomic models: evidence, explanations and limits
concepts.learningGoals: Connect the Dalton, Thomson, Rutherford and Bohr models to the observations they explain. Distinguish a successful prediction from a claim that a historical model describes every feature of an atom.

concepts.title: Waves, orbitals and probability
concepts.learningGoals: Distinguish an orbital from an orbit. Interpret a probability-density representation and explain the uncertainty principle without treating it as merely an instrument defect.

concepts.title: Quantum numbers and electron capacity
concepts.learningGoals: Apply the allowed values of n, ℓ, mℓ and ms. Calculate shell and subshell capacities and identify invalid sets of quantum numbers.

concepts.title: Building electronic configurations
concepts.learningGoals: Use Aufbau, Pauli and Hund together. Translate between shell totals, subshell notation and orbital occupancy without confusing capacity with actual filling order.

concepts.title: Transition atoms, ions and configuration exceptions
concepts.learningGoals: Write the lecturer's chromium and copper exceptions accurately. Construct common ionic configurations and explain why “all cations have a noble-gas configuration” is false.

concepts.title: Reading the periodic table from electronic structure
concepts.learningGoals: Relate periods, groups and blocks to electronic structure. Translate older main-group notation without assigning an incorrect valence count to modern group numbers.

concepts.title: Atomic and ionic size: attraction, shielding and comparison
concepts.learningGoals: Explain broad radius trends using shell extent and effective nuclear attraction. Compare ions correctly, including isoelectronic series, and distinguish different operational radius definitions.

sections.title: Why radius is a defined measurement

concepts.title: Ionisation energies and meaningful exceptions
concepts.learningGoals: Define successive ionisation energies with appropriate gaseous species. Explain broad trends and the Be/B and N/O exceptions, and interpret a large jump in a successive-energy series.

concepts.title: Electron addition, electronegativity and sign conventions
concepts.learningGoals: Distinguish electron affinity from electronegativity. Interpret an explicit electron-addition energy convention and explain why broad trends have exceptions.

concepts.title: Ionic bonding and the whole energy balance
concepts.learningGoals: Explain ionic attraction and charge balance. Use a simple Born–Haber-style energy account without treating electron transfer or an electronegativity cutoff as a complete explanation.

sections.title: From atoms to an extended ionic structure

concepts.title: Covalent structures, octets and formal charge
concepts.learningGoals: Build and check simple Lewis structures. Distinguish electron ownership bookkeeping from the actual distribution of electron density, and recognise octet exceptions without inventing unsupported orbital mechanisms.

concepts.title: Sigma and pi bonds, hybridisation and restricted rotation
concepts.learningGoals: Count sigma and pi bonds in simple molecules. Relate sp, sp² and sp³ models to local geometry and explain why a pi bond constrains molecular shape.

concepts.title: Electron domains, molecular shape and polarity
concepts.learningGoals: Use electron-domain counting to predict simple shapes. Distinguish electron-domain geometry, molecular shape and net dipole, including molecules with polar bonds but no net molecular dipole.

concepts.title: Coordinate bonding and Lewis donor–acceptor chemistry
concepts.learningGoals: Identify the donor and acceptor of an electron pair. Explain NH₄+, H₃O+ and the NH₃–BF₃ adduct without treating a coordinate bond as permanently distinguishable by its origin.

concepts.title: Molecular forces, hydrogen bonds and dissolution
concepts.learningGoals: Compare dispersion, dipole interactions, hydrogen bonding and ion–dipole interactions. Explain solubility and phase behaviour without replacing a full energetic argument with “like dissolves like”.

concepts.title: Constitutional isomers, tautomers and representation
concepts.learningGoals: Distinguish different connectivity from a different drawing of the same molecule. Classify chain, positional and functional isomerism, and explain why tautomerism differs from resonance.

sections.title: Same formula does not determine structure

concepts.title: Conformations and rotational energy barriers
concepts.learningGoals: Distinguish conformation from configuration. Use a viewing direction to compare staggered, eclipsed and anti/gauche arrangements without implying that rotation costs no energy.

concepts.title: Geometric isomerism and E/Z assignment
concepts.learningGoals: Recognise when alkene E/Z isomerism is possible. Apply Cahn–Ingold–Prelog priorities independently at each double-bond carbon and distinguish geometric labels from predictions of stability.

concepts.title: Chirality, R/S configuration and optical rotation
concepts.learningGoals: Recognise nonsuperimposable mirror images. Apply introductory R/S priorities with an explicit viewing direction and distinguish absolute configuration, D/L notation and measured optical rotation.

sections.title: Three labels that must remain separate

concepts.title: Multiple stereocentres, meso compounds and racemates
concepts.learningGoals: Classify enantiomeric and diastereomeric relationships. Explain the 2ⁿ maximum, internal symmetry and the difference between an achiral meso compound and an optically inactive racemic mixture.

concepts.title: Functional groups and biochemical behaviour
concepts.learningGoals: Recognise common functional groups in condensed structures. Connect electron distribution, hydrogen bonding, acid–base behaviour and bond context to biological properties without assuming one group determines an entire molecule's behaviour.

concepts.title: Carbohydrate chemistry, classification and biological roles
concepts.learningGoals: Classify a carbohydrate by its functional groups and number of sugar units. Relate carbohydrate structure to energy supply, storage, support and recognition, while distinguishing molecular chemistry from dietary generalisations.

sections.title: Roles and a worked energy calculation

concepts.title: Fischer projections, D/L and sugar stereoisomers
concepts.learningGoals: Read a Fischer projection, identify the D/L reference centre and distinguish enantiomers, diastereomers and epimers. Work out stereoisomer counts without conflating configuration with optical rotation.

sections.title: How to read a sugar Fischer projection
Worked glucose, mannose and galactose comparison

concepts.title: Ring formation, anomers and mutarotation
concepts.learningGoals: Explain intramolecular hemiacetal/hemiketal formation, identify ring size and anomeric carbon, and translate the stated Fischer/Haworth convention. Explain why a free anomeric centre permits mutarotation and reducing behaviour.

sections.title: Why a chain closes into a ring

concepts.title: Oxidised and reduced monosaccharide derivatives
concepts.learningGoals: Distinguish sugar acids by the carbon oxidised, explain carbonyl reduction to alditols and recognise the chemistry behind representative biological applications.

concepts.title: Deoxy, amino, phosphate and glycoside derivatives
concepts.learningGoals: Identify important sugar substitutions and explain how they change charge, recognition or reactivity. Distinguish a phosphate ester, bisphosphate, diphosphate and an anomeric glycoside.

sections.title: Replacing an OH or adding an amino group
Turning a hemiacetal into a glycoside

concepts.title: Important monosaccharides and biological applications
concepts.learningGoals: Compare glucose, fructose, galactose, ribose and deoxyribose. Explain biological examples while distinguishing a biochemical defect from unsupported universal clinical claims.

sections.title: Lactose hydrolysis and galactose handling are different

concepts.title: Glycosidic notation, reducing ends and condensation arithmetic
concepts.learningGoals: Read linkage notation, locate free anomeric centres and explain reducing behaviour. Calculate the bond and water counts for a specified connected carbohydrate structure.

sections.title: Read both carbon numbers and configuration
Find the reducing centre by chemistry

concepts.title: Disaccharides: structure, digestion and comparison
concepts.learningGoals: Compare maltose, lactose, sucrose, cellobiose and isomaltose. Explain why linkage recognition changes digestibility and why lactose intolerance differs from milk allergy or galactosaemia.

concepts.title: Polysaccharide architecture: starch, glycogen and branching
concepts.learningGoals: Classify glycans by composition and topology. Explain the structures of amylose, amylopectin and glycogen and connect branching to mobilisation without confusing reducing and nonreducing ends.

sections.title: Worked branch counting with stated assumptions

concepts.title: Storage-glucan cleavage and the iodine comparison
concepts.learningGoals: Distinguish hydrolysis from phosphorolysis and explain endo/exo action. Interpret the iodine–starch result as a conformation-dependent signal rather than a universal carbohydrate test.

sections.title: Why iodine produces a starch-associated colour

concepts.title: Structural, microbial and other important glycans
concepts.learningGoals: Relate glycosidic geometry to structural strength and compare cellulose, chitin, peptidoglycan, lipopolysaccharide and selected algal glycans. Preserve organism and matrix-specific qualifications.

sections.title: Other source examples and naming limits

concepts.title: Glycoproteins, proteoglycans and extracellular function
concepts.learningGoals: Distinguish carbohydrate attachment to proteins from the structure of a free polysaccharide. Explain N/O linkage, glycosaminoglycan-rich proteoglycans and how charged chains support hydrated matrices.

concepts.title: Acid-dehydration carbohydrate tests and interpretation
concepts.learningGoals: Compare Molisch, Bial and Seliwanoff principles and interpret controlled observations without treating a screening colour as unique identification. Distinguish chemical theory from an executed laboratory check.

sections.title: Shared starting chemistry, different colour reagents

concepts.title: Reducing-sugar tests: copper chemistry and timed discrimination
concepts.learningGoals: Explain Benedict, Fehling and Barfoed reactions, predict reducing behaviour from structure and distinguish a timed screen from a definitive identification or clinical measurement.

sections.title: Who is oxidised and who is reduced?
Barfoed uses a controlled rate comparison

concepts.title: Bases, nucleosides and nucleotides
concepts.learningGoals: Identify canonical purines and pyrimidines, distinguish bases from nucleosides and nucleotides, and use sugar/base numbering to locate their bonds.

sections.title: Build the molecule in three stages

concepts.title: Phosphate charge and nucleotide functions
concepts.learningGoals: Explain why phosphate-containing structures are charged and connect nucleotide chemistry with energy coupling, regulation, signalling and coenzymes without attributing every role to every nucleotide.

sections.title: Energy coupling is a whole-reaction comparison

concepts.title: Polynucleotide backbone, directionality and sequence
concepts.learningGoals: Explain the 3′–5′ phosphodiester linkage, read antiparallel sequences and calculate backbone links under stated topology assumptions.

sections.title: Direction comes from asymmetric sugar positions

concepts.title: Base composition, complementarity and Chargaff calculations
concepts.learningGoals: Apply canonical duplex composition constraints, calculate base-pair and hydrogen-bond counts, and identify cases in which the simplified equalities do not apply.

sections.title: Why the equalities require a specified molecule
Composition is not sequence or a universal stability formula

concepts.title: DNA helix geometry, topology and packaging
concepts.learningGoals: Connect duplex geometry with molecular recognition and distinguish local helix forms, global supercoiling and protein-associated packaging without treating terminology as a rigid universal classification.

sections.title: The duplex is more than a hydrogen-bonded ladder
A, B and Z are alternative local helix forms

concepts.title: UV measurements, denaturation and melting temperature
concepts.learningGoals: Interpret A260 measurements, purity ratios, hyperchromicity and melting curves. Perform explicitly calibrated examples while distinguishing calculated values from an executed experiment.

sections.title: Absorbance is useful but not uniquely identifying

concepts.title: Base reactions and RNA backbone susceptibility
concepts.learningGoals: Explain why RNA is particularly susceptible to base-catalysed cleavage and distinguish denaturation, backbone cleavage, glycosidic cleavage and base modification.

sections.title: The neighbouring 2′ OH explains an important difference
Four different meanings of a structural change

concepts.title: RNA folding, mRNA, tRNA and rRNA
concepts.learningGoals: Relate RNA sequence and folding to information transfer, adaptor function and ribosomal catalysis. Read codon/anticodon orientations without assuming that all RNAs encode proteins.

concepts.title: Noncoding RNAs, processing and regulation
concepts.learningGoals: Distinguish noncoding RNA functions, explain snRNA-associated splicing at an introductory level, and avoid treating noncoding as synonymous with useless or every transcript as proven functional.

sections.title: Coding potential and molecular function are separate

concepts.title: Modified bases, purine products and therapeutic analogues
concepts.learningGoals: Distinguish natural base modification, catabolism and structural analogues. Explain representative drug mechanisms through verified chemistry without assuming all analogues act identically or offering treatment recommendations.

sections.title: Two mechanisms show why analogues differ

concepts.title: Amino-acid architecture and stereochemistry
concepts.learningGoals: Identify the common backbone and side chain of an α-amino acid. Distinguish a free amino acid from a residue, explain glycine and proline exceptions, and interpret L/D notation without confusing it with optical rotation.

concepts.title: The twenty common side chains and their chemical behaviour
concepts.learningGoals: Recognise all twenty common residues and their codes. Use functional groups to predict charge, interactions and substitutions, while retaining pH and environment qualifications.

concepts.title: Amino-acid ionisation, buffering and isoelectric calculations
concepts.learningGoals: Track charge as pH changes, use supplied pKa values for simple calculations, distinguish pI from pKa and choose the two dissociations that bracket a net-zero state.

sections.title: Proton transfer changes charge without making a peptide

concepts.title: Dietary amino acids, modified residues and biological derivatives
concepts.learningGoals: Distinguish dietary indispensability from side-chain classification, explain representative residue modifications and separate protein-incorporated residues from derived signalling molecules.

sections.title: Essential depends on organism and supply
Derivatives need not be protein residues

concepts.title: Amino-acid reactions, detection and spectroscopy
concepts.learningGoals: Relate analytical reactions to functional groups, recognise ninhydrin exceptions, distinguish electronic from vibrational absorption and interpret measurements without claiming an experiment was performed.

sections.title: Ninhydrin detects chemistry, not identity by itself
UV and infrared answer different questions

concepts.title: Peptide formation, direction and backbone geometry
concepts.learningGoals: Identify the peptide bond and termini, explain why activation is required in cells, and distinguish restricted amide rotation from the conformational freedom of adjacent backbone bonds.

sections.title: A covalent amide creates a directional chain

concepts.title: Peptide counts, sequence information and hydrolysis limits
concepts.learningGoals: Calculate backbone bonds, water balances and simple sequence spaces. Distinguish composition from sequence and interpret amino-acid analysis with its chemical limitations.

sections.title: Count connections before choosing a formula

concepts.title: Secondary structure: helices, sheets, turns and collagen
concepts.learningGoals: Explain how backbone hydrogen bonds organise local structure, compare α helices and β sheets and distinguish the collagen triple helix from an α helix.

sections.title: Local organisation is more than an overall shape
Worked helix geometry and hydrogen-bond counting
β sheets connect neighbouring backbone strands

concepts.title: Tertiary folding, domains and denaturation
concepts.learningGoals: Explain how a chain forms a functional fold, distinguish structural domains from subunits and compare denaturation, peptide hydrolysis and disulfide reduction.

sections.title: Why a soluble chain often buries nonpolar groups
Membrane and soluble proteins have different surroundings
Denaturation is not the same as digestion
Worked interpretation of a folding experiment

concepts.title: Quaternary structure and cooperative protein assemblies
concepts.learningGoals: Identify subunit composition, distinguish association from one-chain folding and explain how interactions between chains can produce capabilities absent from isolated components.

sections.title: More than one chain creates another structural level
Haemoglobin is a useful comparison with myoglobin
When sequence and assembly become biologically important

concepts.title: Protein functions, conjugates and recognition
concepts.learningGoals: Connect representative protein functions to structural features and distinguish chemical conjugate categories from physiological roles.

sections.title: The same chemical toolkit supports many roles
Conjugate classification asks what accompanies the protein

concepts.title: Choosing and interpreting protein-separation methods
concepts.learningGoals: Match separation methods to size, charge or specific binding, predict simple elution behaviour, and distinguish a purified-looking sample from proven identity and activity.

sections.title: A purification workflow needs a property and a readout
Ion exchange depends on the resin and buffer

concepts.title: Enzymes, activation barriers and equilibrium
concepts.learningGoals: Explain biological catalysis, distinguish kinetic barriers from thermodynamic driving force and calculate a relative catalytic rate from supplied comparable constants.

sections.title: A favourable reaction can still be slow
Catalysts change pathways, not the equilibrium endpoint

concepts.title: Active sites, specificity and catalytic mechanisms
concepts.learningGoals: Relate recognition to active-site chemistry, compare lock-and-key and induced-fit descriptions and explain how catalytic groups can help a reaction proceed.

sections.title: Recognition must support a productive reaction
Worked distinction between binding and turnover

concepts.title: Reaction-based enzyme nomenclature and seven EC classes
concepts.learningGoals: Classify a reaction by what is transformed, interpret an EC identifier and distinguish transfer, hydrolysis, nonhydrolytic cleavage, joining and coupled translocation.

sections.title: Classify the reaction rather than the name alone
Coupled transport needs the full activity

concepts.title: Cofactors, coenzymes and vitamin-derived chemical carriers
concepts.learningGoals: Distinguish apoenzyme, holoenzyme, cofactor and prosthetic group; link representative vitamin precursors to their active carrier forms without treating all vitamins as equivalent cofactors.

concepts.title: Measuring initial rates, enzyme activity and units
concepts.learningGoals: Extract an initial rate from suitable data, distinguish concentration/time from amount/time and convert activity units while retaining assay conditions and blanks.

sections.title: Measure a rate before fitting a mechanism

concepts.title: Deriving the simple Michaelis–Menten rate equation
concepts.learningGoals: Explain the steady-state model, distinguish it from rapid binding equilibrium, derive the hyperbolic rate law and state when applying that law is justified.

sections.title: A simple model and its assumptions
From enzyme conservation to the equation
Km is not always a binding dissociation constant

concepts.title: Working with saturation data and reciprocal plots
concepts.learningGoals: Use the Michaelis–Menten equation in both directions, check units and limiting behaviour, and interpret reciprocal plots without treating them as proof of a unique mechanism.

sections.title: Predict a rate with consistent units
A simple table reveals the shape

concepts.title: Turnover, specificity constants and catalytic-centre counts
concepts.learningGoals: Calculate kcat and kcat/Km with consistent units, distinguish maximal turnover from low-substrate performance and account for multiple catalytic centres in one enzyme molecule.

sections.title: Vmax depends on how much active enzyme is present
Worked comparison that changes with substrate
Avoid interpreting a ratio as a complete mechanism

concepts.title: How pH, temperature and solution conditions affect activity
concepts.learningGoals: Explain environmental effects through ionisation and stability, calculate a conditional Q10 example and distinguish an assay optimum from a universal enzyme constant.

sections.title: Protonation affects more than one molecule
Temperature changes both rate and surviving activity

concepts.title: Reversible inhibition: competitive, mixed and uncompetitive models
concepts.learningGoals: Compare ideal reversible inhibition patterns, calculate apparent parameters with supplied factors and distinguish a kinetic pattern from a proven structural binding site.

sections.title: Define the model before assigning a label

concepts.title: Irreversible and mechanism-based enzyme inactivation
concepts.learningGoals: Distinguish persistent inactivation from reversible inhibition, explain a mechanism-based inhibitor and evaluate recovery or time-dependence experiments without overinterpreting one observation.

sections.title: Loss of active enzyme is a different process
Time and recovery provide complementary evidence

concepts.title: Allostery, cooperativity and feedback control
concepts.learningGoals: Explain how ligand binding can regulate a distant active site, distinguish cooperativity from allostery and separate immediate product inhibition from pathway end-product feedback.

sections.title: Binding at one site can influence another
Cooperative substrate responses require an appropriate model
Feedback differs from merely approaching equilibrium

concepts.title: Covalent modification, enzyme abundance and protein modulators
concepts.learningGoals: Compare reversible phosphorylation with changes in enzyme amount, explain a regulatory protein complex and distinguish kinase and phosphatase chemistry.

sections.title: Protein partners can restrain or enable catalysis
Changing enzyme amount usually involves another timescale

concepts.title: Zymogens, activation cascades and isoenzymes
concepts.learningGoals: Explain why enzymes can be made as inactive precursors, distinguish irreversible proteolytic activation from reversible regulation and interpret isoenzyme composition without making diagnostic claims.

sections.title: Proteolysis can activate rather than merely destroy
Isoenzymes catalyse the same reaction with different molecular forms

figures.title: Geometry and molecular dipoles
figures.description: A linear O=C=O structure above a bent H–O–H structure. Equivalent carbon dioxide dipoles oppose, while water bond dipoles do not cancel.
figures.caption: Original schematic. Equivalent polar bonds can cancel by symmetry; the water angle is represented as 104.5° in this idealised comparison.

figures.title: E and Z but-2-ene
figures.description: Two but-2-ene drawings. In the upper structure both higher-priority methyl groups are above the double bond (Z). In the lower structure the methyl groups lie on opposite sides (E).
figures.caption: Original schematic. CH₃ outranks H independently at each alkene carbon; the descriptor does not by itself establish relative stability.

figures.title: A tetrahedral configuration with hydrogen away
figures.description: Central carbon bears Br upwards, Cl lower-right, F on a solid wedge lower-left and H on a dashed bond upper-left. Hydrogen is away; the projected priority order 1 to 2 to 3 is clockwise, giving R.
figures.caption: Original projection schematic, not a bond-angle scale model. Solid wedge points toward the observer; dashed bond away. Reverse the apparent rotation assignment when priority 4 points toward the observer.

figures.title: Lactic-acid Fischer mirror images
figures.description: Two lactic-acid Fischer projections have COOH above and CH3 below. The upper has H left and OH right; the lower has OH left and H right. Horizontal bonds point toward the observer, vertical bonds away.
figures.caption: Original mirror comparison. OH right versus left specifies the depicted configuration relationship; neither location alone establishes the sign of measured optical rotation.

figures.title: Meso and chiral tartaric-acid structures
figures.description: Two Fischer projections of tartaric acid. The upper has both OH groups on the right, representing meso 2R,3S with internal symmetry. The lower has upper OH right and lower OH left, representing 2R,3R; its 2S,3S mirror is a distinct enantiomer.
figures.caption: Original schematic. Two stereocentres permit up to four configurations, but tartaric-acid symmetry leaves three distinct stereoisomers. The meso form is not a racemic mixture.

elements.text: Meso tartaric acid: whole molecule achiral
One chiral form; its mirror is distinct

figures.title: Glucose, mannose and galactose Fischer comparison
figures.description: Three Fischer projections with CHO above and CH2OH below. D-glucose OH sequence at C2–C5 is right,left,right,right. D-mannose differs at C2 and D-galactose at C4. Horizontal bonds project toward the observer and vertical bonds away.
figures.caption: Original projections. Both epimer comparisons retain the D-reference at C5. OH position does not specify the sign of measured rotation.

figures.title: Selected substituents in D-glucopyranose anomers
figures.description: Two simplified pyranose-ring diagrams show the C5 CH2OH group above. The upper alpha anomer has its C1 OH below, while the lower beta anomer has C1 OH above. Ring oxygen is upper-right. Other OH and H substituents are deliberately omitted.
figures.caption: Original partial Haworth schematics: anomeric OH trans versus cis to the reference CH₂OH in the stated D view. These are not complete stereochemical structures or chair conformations.

elements.text: Reference CH₂OH up; other OH omitted
Reference CH₂OH up; other OH omitted

figures.title: Direction and canonical complementarity
figures.description: A schematic ladder has left strand five-prime at top and three-prime at bottom, sequence A G T C. The right has three-prime at top and five-prime at bottom, aligned T C A G. Writing the partner five-prime to three-prime gives G A C T.
figures.caption: Original direction schematic. Rails represent covalent backbones; dashed links represent pairing, not individual hydrogen-bond counts. Helical shape, atomic detail and stacking are omitted.

figures.title: Baseline-corrected midpoint of an illustrative DNA melting curve
figures.description: A rising A260 signal has low plateau 0.50 and high plateau 0.70. Half their difference gives 0.60, reached at the illustrated 70 degrees Celsius. Dashed guides connect that midpoint with both axes.
figures.caption: Original theoretical example, not measured data. Tm is at half the signal change after the low baseline is accounted for; real curves require appropriate baselines and conditions.

figures.title: Neighbouring-group pathway of RNA alkaline cleavage
figures.description: A five-step flow moves from RNA two-prime hydroxyl through deprotonation and attack on the neighbouring backbone phosphorus to cleavage with a two-prime,three-prime cyclic phosphate and a five-prime hydroxyl fragment. Subsequent hydrolysis opens the cyclic phosphate.
figures.caption: Original mechanism flow, not a full electron-pushing structure or a laboratory record. DNA lacks the 2′ OH for this pathway, but remains susceptible to other damage mechanisms.

figures.title: Charge ladder for a supplied two-group example
figures.description: As pH increases, an illustrative free amino acid changes from NH3+ and COOH, net plus one, to NH3+ and COO−, net zero, then NH2 and COO−, net minus one. The dissociations use supplied pKa 2.4 and 9.6.
figures.caption: Original schematic of predominant states, not a measured titration curve. Zwitterionic net zero retains formal charges; pI uses the two dissociations bracketing that state.

figures.title: Planar amide and neighbouring single bonds
figures.description: A simplified backbone segment shows C alpha to carbonyl C to N to C alpha. The carbonyl oxygen and N–H identify the peptide amide unit; the central C–N connection has restricted rotation. Phi and psi refer to adjacent backbone single bonds, not free rotation of the amide.
figures.caption: Original connectivity schematic; all shown bonds are diagrammatic. Resonance gives partial C–N double-bond character without making the entire folded chain planar.

elements.text: Adjacent Cα bonds permit φ / ψ

figures.title: Helical versus sheet hydrogen-bond patterns
figures.description: The upper relationship labels a helix backbone carbonyl at i hydrogen-bonded to N–H at i+4. Below, two beta strands run in opposing N-to-C directions with schematic cross-strand hydrogen bonds. Dashed lines represent hydrogen bonds, not peptide links.
figures.caption: Original relationship diagram, not a molecular-coordinate drawing. The i+4 rule belongs to the alpha helix; the depicted sheet is antiparallel and not drawn to atomic scale.

figures.title: Four descriptions of protein organisation
figures.description: Primary is the residue sequence, secondary local backbone organisation, tertiary the complete fold of one chain, and quaternary the arrangement of multiple chains. A domain is not automatically a separate chain.
figures.caption: Original hierarchy guide, not a claim that all proteins have four levels or one rigid fold. A single polypeptide can have multiple domains without being a multimer.

figures.title: Lower barrier, unchanged endpoints
figures.description: Two schematic reaction paths share reactant and product free energies. A solid high-barrier path and a dashed lower-barrier catalysed path end at the same product level. The drawing distinguishes activation barrier from reaction free-energy difference.
figures.caption: Original qualitative free-energy schematic in arbitrary units; not measured data and not a complete multistep mechanism. The catalyst changes the route, not the equilibrium free-energy difference.

figures.title: A hypothetical Michaelis–Menten saturation curve
figures.description: A calculated rate curve rises towards a limiting Vmax. With supplied Km 20 micromolar, substrate at 20 gives half of the limiting rate. Dashed guides show the half-rate coordinate; the asymptote is approached rather than reached at a finite substrate concentration.
figures.caption: Original calculated model with supplied Km=20 µM and arbitrary limiting-rate scale, not experimental observations or a universal enzyme curve.

figures.title: A later product can inhibit an earlier pathway step
figures.description: In the hypothetical chain A to B to C to D, a returning regulatory line from D ends in an inhibition bar at the enzyme of the A-to-B step. Feedback controls flux without being the same as changing the equilibrium constant.
figures.caption: Original pathway-control schematic, not an asserted named clinical pathway. The inhibited enzyme need not directly produce D; feedback and reverse-reaction effects are distinct.
